9/2/2026, 9:30:18 PM

Yes — approximately.

In plain text I can reverse the letter order in each triplet so it reads the way the triplet would appear in a mirror. What I cannot do in plain text is truly mirror the glyph shapes themselves.

So this is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{mirror-order approximation}
}
$$

—not a literal visual mirror render.

A couple of important notes

1. Palindromic triplets stay the same

Some forms are unchanged in mirror-order, for example:

$$
והו,\quad ילי,\quad אכא,\quad ייי,\quad ההה
$$

because their letter order is symmetric.

2. Final-letter forms get visually awkward in plain text

Things like:

$$
םמע,\quad ךלנ
$$

look odd because Hebrew has special final forms, and plain text reversal doesn't truly mimic the mirrored glyph behavior.

If you want, I can next give you either:

Option A

the full 216-letter string in mirror-order as one continuous block

Option B

a side-by-side table:

$$
\text{original} \quad | \quad \text{mirror-order}
$$

for all 72

Option C

a more exact image-style mirrored chart layout using monospace formatting

Option D

all of the above

Or:

None of these / missing shape — tell me what kind of mirror presentation you want.
